replies.author: DrehmonGreen
replies.body:
If you read the whole thing it is a remarkably nuanced for a team, and frankly community, that is largely anti-AI - as many others in here point out, too.

I'm active in the community and find myself defending AI a lot against all kinds of ideological and ignorant attacks and virtue signaling. This is not it.

If I were running a repo of this size and a serious maintainer/reviewer bottleneck and had to make some kind of compromise to not get bogged down I would adopt an almost identical policy.

> AI contributions have the added pain of being demoralizing. Reviewing PRs is already tedious work, but it is rewarding because reviewers generally feel that their efforts are contributing to educating a new contributor (who may become a future maintainer/reviewer). If your feedback on PRs is just being absorbed by a machine and not going towards mentoring a potential future maintainer, it becomes much harder to justify spending your free time on PR review.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
So you'd throw out good PRs just because there was AI used in them somewhere?

It takes more effort to review them and scrutinize "Did they use AI so I can deny it!?!?" than it does to review through the lens of "is this valuable code?"

They defined the right problem, but totally missed the mark on the solution.

replies.author: DrehmonGreen
replies.body:
Again, they have a reviewer bottleneck and absolutely need to prioritize PRs so they can get anything done. This means making compromises and you need some kind of ruleset that allows you to rapidly go through these PRs without having to look at them in detail and decide if they are worth investing time in.

A vibe coded PR is a pretty good indicator of a lower quality, less maintainable PR - in general. This is where every software engineer regardless of their stance towards AI would agree. And as I just mentioned the additional factor of maintainer moral when reviewing AI PRs and talking to AI instead of a real person who's gaining experience from this process and might become a future reviewer can't be underestimated.

There are a lot of shitty PRs made by people as well, and there are certainly some good ones made by AI. But if you have to prioritize and pick one, I'm afraid vibe coding is the victim for now.

This may very well change at some point and they explicitly state that they are open to reconsidering their approach in the future.

\>It takes more effort to review them and scrutinize "Did they use AI so I can deny it!?!?" than it does to review through the lens of "is this valuable code?"

No offense, but you clearly have no idea what you're talking about here. It takes a lot of time to understand code other people wrote and the reviewers don't know all the modules by heart. There are a lot of tell tale signs that code was written by AI, but of course in practice your average reviewer won't scrutinize every line either. These rules act as a deterrence and the maintainers and experienced collaborative programmers understand what their limits of enforcement are. There is more being said between those lines that you are missing.

I get where you're coming from, this reads like an anti-AI campaign statement if you don't understand all the technical aspects of large open-source projects. And in this AI witch hunt era we need people who speak up.

But if it's people that get their facts wrong it serves nobody and can even be detrimental to having constructive discussions.

replies.author: Mindestiny
replies.body:
Buddy, I'm an IT director who does a considerable amount of DevOps.  I know how code review works.

You're missing the fundamental point here - if theyve gotten far enough into a PR to be trying to judge if it "smells like AI" or not, then the time is already sunk, but theyre choosing to waste more of it because now they're focused on "do I think AI wrote this" and not "is this code elegant, functional, self documenting, and does it solve the issue or enrich the feature it claims it does".

Those are the important parts.  The most important parts.  Not "I don't like AI so Im going to deny this outright"

They already said they have automated tools in place to block PRs from AI agents auto-submitting.  That's reasonable, that's also not a new rule.  *This* is explicitly them saying they're still going to review your PR, but if we think you had Claude help you're getting rejected even if it works great"

Like... The words are *right there*

replies.author: DrehmonGreen
replies.body:
Sorry, you seemed like a vibe code kiddie to me with an axe to grind because they love AI so much ;)

Then you understand what I'm trying to say: it's not only about what's being   
said but what isn't said. They cannot afford to go through PRs line by line and do detective work to maybe find a block of a couple of lines that seems like it was written by an LLM. And they can't prove it anyway.

This policy is a deterrence to people who post low-effort, vibe coded PRs. It says "even if you try to hide it's been made by AI, we'll figure it out and outright reject it without any discussions". In practice they can't (obviously if they admitted that in this post it would defeat the purpose) but it'll no doubt reduce the amount of incoming slop PRs and also give them something to point to when they reject a PR. So they don't have to have a discussion with what might just be a bot in every individual case. Their calculation is that it saves more time and results in better code quality.

And again, a "good" vibe coded PR may get rejected due to that. But that's part of the calculation here and not an exclusively ideological decision like you want to make it out to be.



Like, when you create a community on a discord server for instance. You'll learn pretty quickly to write down a very strict code of conduct - even if you don't want to in the beginning. Because when it grows you don't want to have dozens of discussions daily, where people try to find loopholes so they can still be assholes and insult people, doing indirect self-promotion, etc..

In practice these strict rules aren't really enforced to the letter, and sometimes it feels like overregulation and can lead to someone getting banned who doesnt necessarily deserve it. But the admins didn't start out like a bunch of power-tripping tyrants - it's just what happens when you have to manage a big community, the rules often seem to restrictive. But whether and to which degree they are enforced is a big part of the equation.

replies.author: MarcMurray92
replies.body:
Have you ever written code? Or worked on a multi contributor project?  
  
It’s their project. They maintain it. If they’ve identified AI slop PRs as a huge drain on resources, they’re entitled to set rules to mitigate that. The policy probably isnt perfect, it’ll evolve over time Id say, but the Godot team doesn’t owe spammers the time it would take to honestly review something that was likely mashed together in under a day. 

They've probably got a list of red flags they check against. If someone competent uses AI to automate repetitive aspects of the work, that probably won’t trigger them. The problem is the vast, vast, vast majority of AI outputs across the internet are absolute trash. Why is some slopper entitled to a thorough review of some code he probably hasn't even read?

I see workslop like this constantly in a professional capacity. Someone mashes the Copilot button to generate something 20 times longer/bigger/more complex than it needs to be, then everybody else has to fish through it to find something of value within all the placeholder boilerplate nonsense. It's a waste of time for everyone on the receiving end, without fail.

The problem is literally inherent to AI because these people would have never been able to submit anything if they didn't have a sycophantic code generator telling them their idea is soooo good and everyone will love it. 

It's very much a new problem and anything bar a ban like above is just incurring costs to a free and open source project so sloppers get to be validated for not learning how to write a line of code.  
  
Specifically, from what I have seen, AI creators don't really...improve the same way normal artists/programmers/creators people do. If someone actually wrote their code, submitted a PR, and got told to fix something before it got merged, they've learned something.

Some dude pasting the feedback into Opus and resubmitting the PR 20 minutes later hasn't learned a single thing, all he's done is be more annoying and waste more time. AI users generally don't know how to parse feedback because they usually know so little about the domain they are cosplaying as practitioners of that the feedback is just sort of meaningless to them.  
  
Slop up your own game all you want, go for it, but don't expect other more qualified people to waste their time babysitting some AI bros because they're upset the code they submitted is shit.

comments.author: KindaQuite
comments.body:
* **No autonomous AI agent use or vibe coding**
   * This already leads to an auto-ban from our GitHub repository and will continue to do so.
* **No use of AI to generate substantial pieces of code**
   * We require all code to be human authored. AI assistance should be limited to menial things (like code completion, regex, or find and replace).
   * If you do use AI in some capacity to author code, you must disclose it in the PR discussion.
* **No AI-generated text in human-to-human communication**
   * When our maintainers volunteer their time to review your issue, PR, or proposal, they do not want to talk to a machine. This is a basic principle of respect.
   * Machine translations are still acceptable as long as the original content was written by a human.
* **All PRs must be reviewed and approved by a human before merging**
   * This is the case already, but we will make it more explicit in our policy.

Things change every day with respect to the current suite of AI tools available. We will continue taking a conservative approach in our policies towards them, but we will re-evaluate as things evolve."

This is their bottom line.  
It is not an ideological stance, please stop pushing it like it is.

comments.author: re-skob
comments.body: I understand the burden that is placed on a ton of contributors throwing in 3k line PRs that they barely reviewed themselves for features nobody asked for, but I do wish the Godot team didn't take such a general anti-AI stance. AI coding has invigorated their engine because of how agent friendly it is. ThreeJS recognized this and has been posting lots of pro vibe-coding posts and embracing all of the new AI-empowered devs who are adopting their platform. Godot should do the same - they could actually be eating Unity and Unreal's lunch, even though Unity and Epic have invested millions more in AI integration. Godot has a killer app feature in that all of their files are ascii based - scene files, resource files, and all, so agents can build out full pipelines around Godot and ThreeJS in ways they will never be able to through the binary heavy Unity and Unreal files. I switched exclusively to Godot from Unity because of it.

replies.author: AtlaStar
replies.body:
It literally couldn't be any simpler; godot engine maintainers are tired of dealing with AI pull requests...the people who submit them don't often understand the contributions being made, and the team wants people they can mentor into being maintainers themselves and don't want to sift through slop.

I am not pro AI in the least bit, but how the hell is anyone gonna even be able to tell the contributions are AI if you actually are doing agentic development correctly? AI is entirely capable of writing junior level code for someone who knows that they are doing, but someone who doesn't know how to write a rendering engine shouldn't be telling AI to do it for them no matter how skilled they are if they won't understand the code the AI wrote.

replies.author: franky_reboot

Those are all fair arguments to limit contributions, not denying that. In fact, I admire the goals themselves, in no small part because they proved they mean it.

As I said, I may have been overreacting because I'm very pro-AI (not the blind faith type, of course) and have been sensitive on attacks recently, many were uncalled for. Of course, this right here is one of the healthier approaches.

Maybe the fact good AI code is indistinguishable from good human code yet people attempt at distinctions is what's been bugging me subconsciously and made me overly sensitive.

comments.author: geldonyetich

I heard a lot of complaining about it earlier when I was working with GODOT, and I honestly wondered what the red hot hurry was with iterating the engine that already does everything.

But sounds like what really pushed them over the edge is the pull request volume was way more than they could handle and they were hoping to use them to foster a support network.

>Reviewing PRs is already tedious work, but it is rewarding because reviewers generally feel that their efforts are contributing to educating a new contributor (who may become a future maintainer/reviewer). If your feedback on PRs is just being absorbed by a machine and not going towards mentoring a potential future maintainer, it becomes much harder to justify spending your time on PR review.

Honestly it reads to me like a fundamental difference in philosophy as to how they want to run their open source project. I guess when you get big enough, beggars can be choosers.

comments.author: LexLow
comments.body:
My experience and stories from friends working in more stressful /high-stakes industries as programmers/engineers: 

AI is making code review excruciating.  Especially when the people using it keep letting terrible things through despite test regimines, thus damaging major customer relationships. And then the people who havent given their programming skills over to AI cognitive debt have to muddle through fixing it. 

And in my exp, the people letting terrible bugs into our code base, the ones with permission to experiment with AI workflows, are a select group of senior devs.   And it still leads to nightmare scenarios

There's a difference between using AI to code some gimmicky life-hack Google Playstore app, and using it to make a tool that is going to be long-lived and service millions of people. If Godot wants to survive, it's going to have to aim to be the latter
